Look for the math

The original page makes a surprising claim: this impossible frame is built from two ordinary 3D letters Pi, not from two impossible forks. The logic test checks the drawing that the Java applet actually makes and confirms the structural part of that claim.

The exact claim on the page

Bogomolny wrote: This impossible frame is a combination of two 3D letters Pi. I first thought of it as a pair of impossible forks glued together but later realized that, for its construction, two perfectly possible shapes will suffice. The applet has no text of its own to contradict this. In every one of the 251 slider settings and four canvas sizes tested, the right-hand half is exactly the half-turn image of the left: the same possible piece twice, not two different shapes. Each half's bar is made from two slanted steps and its two beams have equal length, so either half alone is an ordinary object. The impossibility appears only when the two copies are coupled.

How the applet draws it

The canvas divides its height into t = height / 7. Its slanted steps are a = (t/2, -t/sqrt(3)) and b = (-t/2, -t/sqrt(3)); the seven points of one half use only these steps and their sums. The other half is q = (2*cx - x, 2*cy - y), a half-turn about the canvas centre. A beam from p towards q stops at

p + (q - p) * L / distance(p, q)
L = distance(p2, q8) * W / 1000,  250 ≤ W ≤ 500

At W = 500 the length L is exactly half the distance between p8 and q2, so two opposing beams finish at the same point: the halves join. For smaller W a gap remains and the applet paints two small faces over the edges behind them. The test compares all 251 values of W, both edge modes and four canvas sizes with a second transcription of the bytecode; every point, face and line agrees.

Why one flat picture can tell two stories

A point on the page does not say how far away it is. Adding the same amount to all three depth coordinates moves a point nowhere on the flat page, so the left half can be read with one depth order and the right half with the opposite one. Each reading is fine on its own; demanding both at the joined ends at once is not. Pressing Show the rear edges draws the lines the default picture masks, which is the applet's LessReal = 1 mode. The behaviour here matches the Java applet; only the presentation changed, with a slider and a draggable dot in place of its scrollbar and a modern SVG board in place of its AWT canvas.

Set Visible gap, then drag the bottom dot slowly right until the two beams meet under the green dot. Look at each half on its own: can you see why each piece could be built, but not both at once?
